doc.title: Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 30, 2009

title: The Holy Roller church and the 'Unknown Tone'
summary: Ali describes intense church music, people falling out, and a similar seizure at a concert in Italy.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: I wanted to back up just a little bit. You said your family, was it Baptist? You said Holy Roller I think.
Yeah right. We used to say Holy Roller, so that’s like Baptist.
And the music in that church was probably pretty upbeat.
Very upbeat. I mean they used to like go nuts in there. I mean you ever heard of a thing called the Unknown Tone?

They would get so religious and so carried away with the music until sometimes they would just faint, fall out, and then they would go start babbling [scats] stuff that you didn’t even know what they were and sometimes they would have like a seizure and foam would be coming out of their mouth. And I mean that was very intense stuff. And even it didn’t matter what age they were, I mean it’d be from older people to little kids who were actually — you know something like that happened to me when I was in Italy one night. Sonny Fortune and I was playing in Italy one night. And at times we used to play. I mean this is recent, maybe a couple of years ago, three or four years ago. We used to play very intense stuff. Like we would play a song, really uptempo, and we would play it for the whole set without stopping. We’d play for an hour, hour and twenty minutes. Uptempo, like “Impressions” or something, for the whole set. We’d do it for the whole set. Just the two of us — saxophone and drums. Right? And this woman was right in front of us and she stood up and fell straight back and was into convulsions and stuff. And that reminded me of when it happened in the church when I was coming up, right? She was just sitting there then all of a sudden she just leaped up in the air and screamed and fell back. And we didn’t really stop, but we was on our way to stopping. And they took her out like into the restroom area and she was laid down. And we kind of came to the end of the song, and I rushed back there to see what was with her, and I looked down at her and she was just, she was kind of okay a little bit. She said, “It was the music, the music, it just like, it just” I mean she actually did one of those seizure things. Right? And I used to see that happen in the church on Sundays. Not every Sunday but sometimes they get really intense and the tambourines would be going and the people would be singing and their music would be happening, and somebody would just, “Ohhh” you know. I’ve seen that a lot of times. They used to call that the “Unknown Tone.” © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
Okay. And did they have another term for it, like, you know, Doris got the spirit or something?

Yeah, that’s what it was. I mean you know, but actually, it was like a seizure or something. You know, it was just caught up in whatever it was and just fell out. And maybe not completely fall out, but just start babbling and — but not only that but they had on staff a lot of those black churches, they had to have nurses on staff where they would actually come out and get people. They had their white gowns on and stuff, they’d come out and get people and take them to where they can rest. And they had nurses there to take care of these people. Because they were just like in those Baptist churches, we used to call them Holy Rollies as kids, right? They would just go out. The music. And it’s usually the music that gets them, and the playing and the praying and the preacher would be repetitiously saying these things over and over and over again, and the music would be going on and the choir would be singing, and all of this would be going on and then somebody would just go, “Ohhhh.” It was intense. Unbelievable stuff.
Did that stuff find its way into your drumming?

I think all of it had something to do with it. You know. I mean my whole life had something to do with what I do for a living. But that was some intense stuff. And I actually saw that happen, and when it happened in Italy, I was like wow, this is for real.
